STATEMENT OF ASSIGNMENTS OF ERROR
First Assignment of Error: The trial court erred in refusing to allow defendant-appellant to withdraw the admissions that were based on defendant's belated response to the request for admissions. Judgment and Entry of August 13, 2007:
Second Assignment of Error: The trial court erred in granting summary judgment to plaintiff on his claims and on defendant's counterclaims. Judgment and Entry of August 13, 2007.
1

STATEMENT ON SUMMARY JUDGMENT
The summary judgment is inappropriate as a matter of law, because the trial court erred in refusing to permit defendant to withdraw the admissions.
If defendant were permitted to withdraw the admissions, all the material facts would be disputed, such as the amount that defendant owes plaintiffs, whether plaintiffs locked the premises in order to force defendant from the premises, and whether defendant abandoned the premises.

ISSUES PRESENTED FOR REVIEW
Whether the trial court erred in refusing to allow defendant-appellant to withdraw the admissions. First Assignment of Error.
Whether the trial court erred in granting summary judgment. Second Assignment of Error.
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
On January 19, 2007, Plaintiffs-Appellees, Allison Bush and Kimberly Malkowski (hereinafter "Plaintiffs") filed a Complaint against Defendant-Appellant, Edward Eckman (hereinafter "Eckman" or "Defendant"). The Complaint alleged two causes of action, (1) forcible detainer and entry and, (2) a claim for monetary damages. On February 6, 2007, Defendant filed a timely Answer. Defendant raised affirmative defenses of waiver and estoppel in addition to violations of Ohio Revised Code ("O.R.C") sections 5321.04(A)(8) and 5321.15, entering Defendant's premises without notice and preventing Defendant from having access to the premises for purposes of recovering possession, respectively. Defendant also asserted several counterclaims for violations of O.R.C. 5321.04(A)(8), O.R.C. 5321.15, conversion and loss of use of premises, loss of belongings and emotional and mental distress. By agreement of the parties, Defendant left the premises, thus mooting out the forcible entry and detainer action. Judgment Entry, p.1. Therefore, the only claims that remained were Plaintiff's claim for damages and defendant's counterclaim.
On April 3, 2007, plaintiffs served on defendant discovery that included requests for admission. On June 5, 2007, plaintiffs moved for summary judgment, based primarily on the request for admissions. On July 10, 2007, defendant responded to the request for admissions, denying each request for admissions. On July 18, 2007, plaintiff filed a timely Memorandum Contra the Motion for Summary Judgment. Plaintiff attached the response to the request for admissions and answers
3

:
to interrogatories and asked the trial court for permission to withdraw the admissions. On July 24, 2007, plaintiff filed a reply to the Memorandum Contra the Motion for Summary Judgment .. The trial court on August 13, 2007 filed a judgment entry granting plaintiff's motion for summary judgment The trial court, without citing any case authority, granted the summary judgment entirely based on the fact that defendant filed the admissions contra to the rules. Judgment Entry, p. 2. The trial court awarded Plaintiffs $995.40 plus interest and dismissed defendant's counterclaim
STATEMENT OF FACTS
On September 25, 2006, Defendant Edward Eckman entered into a lease agreement with Plaintiff Allison Bush for the premises located at 86 Nautica Way, Buckeye Lake, Ohio 43008 (hereinafter "the premises"). The term began on October 1, 2006 and was to expire on March 31, 2007. Affidavit of Edward Eckman, attached to Defendant's Memorandum Contra Motion for Summary Judgment. However, prior to the expiration of the lease, Plaintiffs unlawfully entered the premises without providing notice to Eckman. Then Plaintiffs changed the locks to the premises. Thereafter, Eckman was prevented from having access to the premises. He was not given keys to the new locks. Nor did Eckman receive any note from the Plaintiffs relating to contact information if he "returned" to the property. Eckman was not able to recover possession of the premises or of his personal belongings. Affidavit of Edward Eckman
Eckman never abandoned the premises. At no time did he leave the premises unlocked. In addition, Eckman never told the Plaintiffs that he was not coming back to the premises.
ARGUMENT
I. FIRST ASSIGNMENT OF ERROR-THE TRIAL COURT ERRED IN REFUSING TO ALLOW DEFENDANT-APPELLANT TO WITHDRAW THE ADMISSIONS THAT WERE BASED ON DEFENDANT'S BELATED RESPONSE TO THE REQUEST
4
0

--
FOR ADMISSIONS.
The trial court held that the request for admissions would be considered admitted, because defendant served the response to the request for admissions late and did not request leave of the court in order to do so. Based on the admissions, the trial court granted judgment to plaintiff on both his claims and on defendant's counterclaims. Defendant had asked the trial court to allow defendant to amend the responses so that he could deny the requests for admissions in accordance with the evidence. Defendant also filed with his memorandum contra Plaintiffs' Motion for Summary Judgment Defendant's Response to Plaintiffs' Request for Admissions and Interrogatories.
The trial court in his judgment entry did not even comment on defendant's request to withdraw the admissions and did not consider the case law, including decisions by this Court, that indicated that a trial court should allow a party to amend or withdraw the response to the request for admissions. Instead, the trial court stated that "the Court is not considering the discovery materials filed without leave and is basing it's ruling in favor of the Plaintiff, primarily on the fact that the Defendant failed to comply with the rules." The trial court then granted judgment to Plaintiffs and dismissed defendant's counterclaim. Judgment Entry, p. 2.
Ohio R.Civ. P. 36(B) allows a party to withdraw or amend the admissions. Rule 36(B) states that "(s)ubject to the provisions of Civ. R. 16 governing modification of a pretrial order, the court may permit withdrawal or amendment (of admissions) when the presentation of the merits of the action will be subserved thereby and the party who obtained the admission fails to satisfy the court that withdrawal or amendment will prejudice the party in maintaining his action or defense on the merits." See Balson v. Dodds (1980), 62 Ohio St.2d 287, 405 N.E.2d 293 and Kutscherousky v.
5
0

Integrated Communications Solutions, LLC, et al. (5th Dist. 2005), 2005 WL 1985228, 2005-Ohio- 4275, 116 (Unreported) (attached to this brief). As this Court stated, "(t)he above standard set forth in Civ. R. 36 makes no mention of 'excusable neglect." It "does not require that a written motion be filed and does not specify when such motion must be made." Kutscherousky v. Integrated Communications Solutions, LLC, et al., supra, [17. Furthermore, "by contesting the truth of the Civ.R.36(A) admissions, for the purposes of summary judgment, the party "satisfied the requirement of Civ.R. 36(B) that the party move the trial court to withdraw or amend the admissions." Id.
The Ohio Supreme Court has held that "(t)his provision emphasizes the importance of having the action resolved on the merits, while at the same time assuring each party that justified reliance on an admission in preparation for trial will not operate to his prejudice." Cleveland Trust Co. v. Willis (1985), 20 Ohio St.3d 66,67, 485 N.E.2d 1052, 1053. In essence, courts, including this Court, have held that there is a two-prong test for determining whether withdrawal or amendment of a request for admissions should be allowed. "First, the court must look to whether the 'presentation of the merits will be subserved' by allowing the amendment. Second, the court must address whether the withdrawal will prejudice the party that has obtained the admissions." Kutscherousky v. Integrated Communications Solutions, LLC, supra, 118.
Under the first prong, courts have held that in "(p)lacing the definition in the context of the Civ. R. 36 test, the burden is on the moving party to show how withdrawal or amendment of the admissions would assist in reaching a just resolution of the action on its merits. With regard to this, the federal courts have held that this burden is clearly met when the effect of denying a motion to withdraw and amend would 'practically eliminate any presentation of the merits." Id, 119.
6

In this case, the trial court, by denying defendant the opportunity to amend the admissions prevented defendant from presenting the merits of the case. Material facts are in dispute in this case. For example, whether Eckman owes Plaintiffs any monies, whether Eckman abandoned the premises, whether Eckman was given new keys to allow him access to the premises and whether Eckman told Plaintiffs he was not returning to the premises are all in dispute. By not allowing defendant to withdraw or amend the admission, defendant was prevented from presenting independent evidence to oppose summary judgment on the claim and counterclaim.
This Court has held that the second prong of the test "'relates to the difficulty a party may face in proving its case' because of the sudden need to obtain evidence required to prove the matter that had been admitted." Kutscherousky v. Integrated Communications Solutions, LLC, supra, 125. In order for the plaintiff to prove prejudice it is not sufficient for the plaintiff to have to "convince the trier of fact of the truth of a matter erroneously admitted." Id. (citations omitted) Furthermore, " ... preparing a summary judgment motion in reliance upon an erroneous admission does not constitute prejudice." Id. In addition, this Court has held that " ... where a party all but conceded liability through its admission in a contested case, it is unlikely that the opposing party could have reasonably relied on the truth of the admission. Id.
Here, withdrawal of the admissions could not prejudice the Plaintiffs in any way. Plaintiff did not present any evidence to the trial court that it would be prejudiced by permitting defendant to amend or withdraw the admissions. The trial court did not even consider whether plaintiff would be prejudiced by the withdrawal of the admissions. There is no prejudice to the plaintiff. Discovery had not been completed. The trial was scheduled to occur some months after defendant had requested that he be permitted to withdraw the admissions. In addition, Eckman had responded to
7
0

all discovery propounded by the Plaintiffs, including the Request for Admissions, documents requested, and answers to interrogatories. Plaintiffs had ample time to prepare the case for trial. Furthermore, Plaintiffs could not reasonably have relied on the truth of the admissions. Plaintiffs' Request for Admissions asked for admissions on key facts that went to the heart of this case. If Defendant had admitted each admission, he would have effectively conceded liability. Plaintiffs could not have reasonably relied on the admissions under these circumstances.
As was true in Kutscherousky, supra, the trial court abused its discretion in not allowing defendant to withdraw the admissions. The trial court has prevented defendant from proving his case. The withdrawal of the admissions would not have prejudiced Plaintiffs in any way. This is not a case in which defendant asked that the admissions be withdrawn on the eve of trial or on the first day of trial, in which Plaintiffs could have legitimately argued that it was prejudiced by the withdrawal. Furthermore, Defendant has not defied the court's discovery orders. See, Kutscherousky v. Integrated Communications Solutions, LLC, et al., supra, 122.
II. SECOND ASSIGNMENT OF ERROR-THE TRIAL COURT ERRED IN GRANTING SUMMARY JUDGMENT TO PLAINTIFF ON HIS CLAIMS AND ON DEFENDANT'S COUNTERCLAIMS
Plaintiffs' summary judgment motion is based on Plaintiff Bush's affidavit and on the admissions. However, the facts sworn to in Eckman's affidavit are contrary to those in Plaintiff's affidavit. In addition, Eckman has denied each of Plaintiffs' requests for admissions. Without Eckman's admissions, there are genuine issues of material fact on Plaintiffs' Claims as well as Defendant's Counterclaims. For example, Plaintffs argue that Eckman abandoned the premises and that after Plaintiffs changed the locks to the premises, Eckman was still given access to the premises by the Plaintiffs. To support this assertion, Plaintiffs cited to the admissions. However, because
8

.
Eckman has denied these admissions, there exist genuine issues of material fact. Furthermore, Plaintiffs argue that Eckman has no claim for conversion or emotional distress. Once again Plaintiffs cited to the admissions for this assertion. However, Eckman has denied these admissions. Therefore, this Court should reverse the summary judgment and have the case decided by the trier of fact.
CONCLUSION
For the foregoing reasons, the decisions of the trial court denying permission to withdraw the admissions and granting summary judgment should be reversed and the case remanded for a trial on the merits of the claims and counterclaims.

JUDGMENT ENTRY
This matter came on for the Court's consideration upon the Plaintiffs' Motion for Summary Judgment on their Complaint and the Defendant's Counterclaim. Plaintiff asserts that there are no genuine issues of material fact and as a result, they are entitled to judgment, as a matter of law, on their Complaint and also on the Defendant's Counterclaim.
This case was commenced January 19, 2007, upon the Plaintiffs filing a Complaint seeking to evict the tenant from property located in Buckeye Lake, Ohio. In addition to seeking restitution of the premises, Plaintiffs also sought money damages.
On February 6, 2007, the First Claim of the Plaintiffs was resolved by mutual agreement between the parties, by way of an Agreed Entry signed by Judge W. David Branstool on that date. Thereafter, on February 6, 2007, the Defendant filed a timely Answer and Counterclaim to the Plaintiffs' Complaint. On February 27, 2007, an Agreed Entry was submitted to the Court granting Plaintiffs an extension of time to move or plead to the Counterclaim. On March 14, 2007, Plaintiffs filed a Reply to the Defendant's Counterclaim, and also their amended Complaint.
A pre-trial was set for April 5, 2007. However, it was continued by mutual consent of the parties. Also, on April 4, 2007, the Defendant was served, through his attorney, with Requests for Admission, Interrogatories and Document Requests.
On May 3, 2007, a pre-trial was held in an attempt to resolve various issues outstanding in this case. On June 11, 2007, Plaintiffs filed a Motion for

Summary Judgment on both the Complaint and the Defendant's Counterclaim. On July 18, 2007, counsel for the Defendant filed responses to the Requests for Admission, Interrogatories and for the Production of Documents, along with the Defendant's Memorandum Contra to the Plaintiff's Motion for Summary Judgment.
Defendant was given ample time under the Rules of Procedure, to file responses to the Interrogatories and Requests for Admission. At no time did the Defendant seek an extension of time from the Court to answer Interrogatories and provide Admissions or Denials to Requests for Admission. In fact, it wasn't until Plaintiff filed a Motion for Summary Judgment that the Defendant attempted, without leave of Court, to file Answers to Interrogatories and responses to Requests for Admission. Accordingly, the Court is not considering the discovery materials filed without leave and is basing it's ruling in favor of the Plaintiff, primarily on the fact that the Defendant failed to comply with the rules. Requests for Admission not denied, are admitted.
IT IS HEREBY ORDERED, ADJUDGED AND DECREED that Plaintiffs are awarded $995.40 plus interest accruing from the date of judgment and costs. It is further ordered that the Defendant's Counterclaim is hereby dismissed.
Judge W. David Branstool
